unit.title: Provide financial and business performance information

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Nordia Campbell is asked to supply monthly performance information to the new operations manager of a Kingston logistics firm. What should she do first?
options: Send him the same pack she gives the finance director
Ask him which decisions the information must support
Pick the measures that are easiest to take from the system
Wait until he complains about figures that are missing

questions.stem: Why might the general manager and a front-desk supervisor at the same hotel need different performance information?
options: Because the supervisor may not see any figures at all
Because only managers can understand financial terms
Because each decides at a different level and time span
Because the hotel's system can print only one report each

questions.stem: After agreeing a manager's needs, what should the information specification record?
options: Each measure, its source, format, frequency and due date
The staff who will be blamed if figures are late
Only the total sales figure and the bank balance
The preparer's own views on the manager's style

questions.stem: The director of a public agency asks for "everything about costs". What is the best response?
options: Send every ledger entry for the year as a spreadsheet
Refuse until the request is put in writing by the board
Send last year's annual report, which covers all costs
Clarify which cost decisions she must make

questions.stem: Which user of a firm's performance information is most interested in whether the firm can repay its loan on time?
options: The lender that provided the loan
The marketing team planning a campaign
A customer making a one-off purchase
A new trainee in the stores section

questions.stem: Which is an internal source of financial performance information?
options: The central bank's published inflation figures
A competitor's advertised prices for the season
The firm's general ledger and sales records
A trade association's yearly survey of its members

questions.stem: A clinic manager in May Pen wants to know how long patients wait to be seen. Where is this data most likely to come from?
options: The time records in the check-in system
The payroll records for the nursing staff
The clinic's register of fixed assets
The bank statements for the clinic's account

questions.stem: Odane Brown needs last quarter's electricity cost for each branch. One branch's bill was coded to the wrong account in the ledger. What should he do?
options: Use the ledger as it is, since it is the official record
Leave that branch out of the report without comment
Estimate the branch's cost from the other branches
Have the coding corrected and use the corrected figure

questions.stem: March's sales are being reported on 3 April, but some sales made on 31 March have not yet been entered. What is the best approach?
options: Report only the sales entered and say nothing more
Enter the missing sales, or note their estimated value
Move the missing sales into April's figures instead
Hold back the whole report until the end of April

questions.stem: Which check best confirms that the total sales figure in a performance report is accurate?
options: Ask a colleague whether the figure looks about right
Compare it with the figure in last year's report
Agree it to the ledger and the sales system totals
Round it to the nearest million so small errors vanish

questions.stem: A draft report shows cleaning costs of J$4,500,000 for one month, against about J$450,000 in every other month. What should the preparer do first?
options: Send it, since managers can spot their own errors
Replace it with the average of the other months
Delete the line so that the total looks normal
Check the entry, as it may be a keying error

questions.stem: Several staff add data to one shared monthly spreadsheet. What best protects the accuracy of the figures?
options: Let anyone overwrite a formula when they need to
Lock the formula cells and keep a log of changes
Save a separate copy on each person's own laptop
Remove the totals so that no formula can break

questions.stem: Sales were J$12,000,000 and cost of sales was J$7,800,000. What is the gross profit margin?
A Spanish Town wholesaler reports current assets of J$3,600,000 against current liabilities of J$2,400,000. What current ratio should the report show?
A retailer's current ratio has fallen from 1.8 to 0.9 in a year. What does this most likely tell the manager?
options: The firm has become much more profitable
It may struggle to pay its short-term debts
Its staff costs have fallen sharply this year
Its long-term loans have now been fully repaid

questions.stem: Sales rose from J$40,000,000 last year to J$46,000,000 this year. What is the percentage growth?
Sales grew by 15%, but gross profit in J$ stayed the same as last year. What should the report point out?
options: That the business is doing better on every measure
That sales staff should be given a bonus at once
That the gross margin has fallen and needs looking at
That the cost of sales must have fallen this year

questions.stem: Trade receivables are J$3,000,000 and yearly credit sales are J$36,500,000. Using a 365-day year, what are the debtor (receivable) days?
options: 30 days
12 days
45 days
122 days

questions.stem: Why is a single month's figure usually less useful to a manager than a twelve-month trend?
options: Because monthly figures are never checked by anyone
Because one month may be skewed by one-off events
Because managers may not see monthly figures
Because a trend needs no source data behind it

questions.stem: A Negril hotel's revenue in September is far below August. Which comparison gives the manager the fairest view of September?
options: September against the best month of the year
September against the yearly average of all hotels
September against the budget set for August
September against September of last year

questions.stem: A department's budget for the quarter was J$2,500,000 and actual spending was J$2,800,000. By what percentage was it over budget?
A call centre in Montego Bay wants one measure of the service its callers receive. Which is the best KPI (key performance indicator)?
options: Total number of calls received each month
Average length of each agent's lunch break
Share of calls answered within the target time
Number of new headsets bought this year

questions.stem: Which is a leading indicator of next quarter's sales for a firm that supplies other businesses?
options: Last quarter's profit after tax
The number of quotations sent this month
Last year's total sales revenue
Bad debts written off last year

questions.stem: A hotel had 2,000 room-nights available in a month and sold 1,700 of them. What was its occupancy rate?
Why should a performance pack for a school board include measures such as attendance and examination results?
options: Because financial figures cannot be checked
Because the law forbids reporting money alone
Because they show if the school meets its purpose
Because they take less time to prepare than accounts

questions.stem: A balanced scorecard groups performance measures under four headings. Which set is correct?
options: Financial, customer, internal process, learning and growth
Sales, purchases, wages and taxes
Political, economic, social and technological
Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats

questions.stem: A parish council compares its cost of collecting garbage per household with the same cost at three similar councils. What is this called?
options: Forecasting
Auditing
Budgeting
Benchmarking

questions.stem: Which display best shows how monthly revenue has moved over the last two years?
options: A pie chart of each month's share
A line graph across the 24 months
A single table of the two yearly totals
A map showing where the branches are

questions.stem: A busy director wants to see only the items that need her attention. Which approach suits her best?
options: Exception reporting of items outside agreed limits
A full printout of every account in the ledger
A spoken update with no figures in it at all
A single report sent once the year has ended

questions.stem: Why should a performance report include a short written commentary as well as the tables?
options: To make the report look longer and more thorough
To replace the figures, which managers rarely read
To explain the causes of key movements
To record the preparer's views on other departments

questions.stem: The vertical axis of a bar chart starts at J$9,000,000 instead of zero, so a small rise looks huge. What is the problem?
options: The chart uses too many different colours
The bars should have been drawn in 3-D
The data should have gone in a pie chart
It exaggerates the change and may mislead

questions.stem: Shanice Reid must present the quarter's results to the board of a community co-operative whose members are not accountants. What should she do?
options: Use technical terms so the board trusts her figures
Use a few clear charts and explain key terms simply
Hand out the full trial balance without any comment
Leave out any figure that shows the co-op made a loss

questions.stem: Which presentation choice helps managers compare figures quickly across a monthly report?
options: The same units, periods and layout on every page
Different currencies on alternate pages
Every figure shown down to the last cent
A fresh layout each month to keep interest

questions.stem: The monthly performance pack reaches managers 25 days after the month ends. What is the main problem?
options: The figures will be more accurate than they need
Managers will have too long to read the pack
It comes too late for managers to act on it
Finance staff will have little to do meanwhile

questions.stem: A manager needs a sales figure by noon for a pricing decision, but full checks take two days. What is the best course?
options: Give no figure at all until every check is done
Give an early figure, clearly marked as unchecked
Give last month's figure as if it were current
Give a figure without saying how it was made

questions.stem: A supervisor with no authority to see pay data asks Ricardo, a finance officer, for a report of each staff member's salary. What should Ricardo do?
options: Send it, as the supervisor is senior to him
Send it with names removed but job titles shown
Ask a co-worker to send the report instead
Decline and refer him to the authorised manager

questions.stem: A report on customer accounts is to be emailed to managers. Which step best fits the general aims of the data protection law?
options: Include only the personal data each manager needs
Copy all staff so that nobody misses it
Add customers' home addresses to be complete
Send it from a personal account to save time

questions.stem: A manager asks the analyst to leave out a large loss so that the quarter "looks better" for the board. What should the analyst do?
options: Leave it out, since the manager carries the blame
Move the loss quietly into next quarter's figures
Keep it in and report the request upward
Show the loss only in a small footnote at the back

questions.stem: A director queries a figure in the pack the day after it is issued. What should the preparer do?
options: Tell her the figure is right without checking
Leave the query until the next pack is due
Change it to the figure the director expected
Check the source, reply and correct if needed

questions.stem: How can the information officer best find out whether the monthly pack meets managers' needs?
options: Ask users which items they use and which they miss
Count the number of pages in the pack each month
Check once a year whether the pack was sent on time
Compare its length with packs from other firms

questions.stem: Managers say they never use eight of the twenty measures in the monthly pack. What is the best response?
options: Add more measures so that the pack is complete
Agree with users to drop or replace those measures
Keep all twenty, since they took effort to build
Stop sending the pack to managers who complain

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of a dashboard linked directly to the firm's accounting system?
options: It removes the need for any checking of the data
It lets every member of staff change the figures
It gives managers current figures on demand
It means monthly accounts no longer need preparing

questions.stem: Two branches each made J$1,800,000 net profit. Branch A had sales of J$24,000,000 and Branch B had sales of J$12,000,000. Which statement is correct?
options: Both branches performed equally well
Branch B earned the higher net profit margin
Branch A earned the higher net profit margin
No margin can be worked out from this data

questions.stem: A training agency spent J$18,000,000 on a programme that 600 trainees completed. What was the cost per trainee who completed?
A performance report includes a forecast of year-end profit. What must it also show so that managers can judge the forecast?
options: The main assumptions behind it
The names of all who typed the figures
Every forecast from the past ten years
The preparer's full job description

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A manager tracks "percentage of invoices paid within 30 days" each month against a target. What three-letter short form names this kind of measure?
Sales were J$20,000,000 and gross profit was J$6,000,000. What is the gross profit margin, as a percentage?
For the board pack, work out the current ratio from current assets of J$5,000,000 and current liabilities of J$2,000,000.
What one-word name is given to a screen that shows a manager's key measures together, often as charts and dials?
Sales rose from J$25,000,000 to J$28,000,000. What is the percentage increase?
A store handled 12,000 transactions in a month and received 18 complaints. How many complaints is that per 1,000 transactions?
Receivables are J$2,250,000 and yearly credit sales are J$18,250,000. Using a 365-day year, how many debtor days is this?
What one-word name is given to the process of comparing two sets of records, such as the ledger and the sales system, to make sure they agree?
What two-word term names the record that lets a reported figure be traced back to its source documents?
Which chart, drawn as a circle cut into slices, shows how a total is split into its parts?
What one-word term names the difference between a budgeted figure and the actual figure for the same period?
Net profit was J$2,400,000 on sales of J$30,000,000. What is the net profit margin, as a percentage?
The quick (acid-test) ratio leaves out one current asset because it may take time to turn into cash. Which asset is it?
Staff numbers averaged 40 during the year and 6 people left. What was the staff turnover rate, as a percentage?
Sales for three months were J$4,200,000, J$3,900,000 and J$4,500,000. What was the average monthly sales figure, in J$?

essays.stem: You have been asked to provide financial and business performance information to the managers of a medium-sized manufacturing firm in St Catherine. Explain how you would find out what information each manager needs.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by listing the people who will use the information: the general manager, the production, sales and human resources managers, and the board. I would meet each one briefly and ask which decisions they make, how often, and what they need to know to make them. For example, the production manager needs output, waste and cost per unit weekly, while the board needs profit, cash and key risks each quarter. I would also read the firm's business plan and budget so that the measures match its goals. From these talks I would draft an information specification for each manager: the measures, the source of each figure, the level of detail, the format, how often it is needed and the deadline. I would check the draft with each manager and agree what is possible with the systems and staff we have. I would also agree who may see sensitive information such as pay. Finally, I would agree a date to review the specification after three months, because needs change as managers use the information.
markingPoints: Identifies the different users and meets them to learn what decisions they make
Links the information to the firm's plans, budget and goals
Records measures, sources, detail, format, frequency and deadlines in a specification
Confirms the specification with each manager, including access to sensitive data
Plans to review the needs after a set period

essays.stem: Describe how you would gather data from different sources and check it before you include it in a monthly business performance report.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would list the data each report line needs and its source: the general ledger for income and costs, the sales system for volumes, the payroll system for staff costs, and operational records such as attendance or complaints logs. I would agree a timetable with the owners of each source so that data reaches me soon after month end. When the data arrives I would check that it covers the full month and that late items, such as sales on the last day, are included or noted. I would reconcile totals between systems, for example sales in the ledger against the sales system, and investigate any difference. I would compare each figure with the previous month, the same month last year and the budget, and query any large or odd movement, as it may be an error rather than a real change. I would check formulas and links in the spreadsheet and ask a colleague to review the key figures. Finally, I would keep notes of sources and adjustments so that every figure can be traced back.
markingPoints: Identifies the sources needed for each item and agrees a timetable with data owners
Checks completeness and cut-off at month end
Reconciles figures between systems and investigates differences
Uses comparisons to spot unusual figures and queries them
Has the work reviewed and keeps an audit trail of sources and adjustments

essays.stem: A firm's sales were J$30,000,000 in Year 1 and J$36,000,000 in Year 2. Cost of sales was J$18,000,000 in Year 1 and J$23,400,000 in Year 2. Net profit was J$3,000,000 in Year 1 and J$2,880,000 in Year 2. Calculate the sales growth and the gross and net profit margins for both years, and write a short commentary for the managing director.
essays.modelAnswer: Sales grew by J$6,000,000, which is 20% of Year 1 sales. Gross profit was J$12,000,000 in Year 1 (J$30,000,000 less J$18,000,000), a gross margin of 40%. In Year 2 it was J$12,600,000 (J$36,000,000 less J$23,400,000), a gross margin of 35%. The net profit margin was 10% in Year 1 (J$3,000,000 out of J$30,000,000) and 8% in Year 2 (J$2,880,000 out of J$36,000,000). Commentary: the firm sold much more in Year 2, but it earned less on each dollar of sales. Cost of sales rose by 30% while sales rose by 20%, so the gross margin fell by five percentage points. Net profit actually fell slightly in J$ despite the extra sales, so overheads also need review. I recommend that management finds out whether the margin fell because of higher supplier prices, discounts given to win the new sales, or more waste, and that prices and purchasing are reviewed before the firm grows further. These figures should be checked against the budget and the market before final decisions are made.
markingPoints: Sales growth correctly worked as 20%
Gross margins correctly worked as 40% and 35%
Net margins correctly worked as 10% and 8%
Explains that sales rose but margins and net profit fell, with costs rising faster than sales
Recommends sensible further investigation or action for the managing director

essays.stem: Compare financial and non-financial performance information, and explain why managers of a Jamaican hotel need both.
essays.modelAnswer: Financial information is expressed in money: revenue, costs, profit, cash and ratios such as gross margin. It comes mainly from the accounts, can be checked against the ledger and shows the results of past decisions. Its limit is that it often arrives after the month has ended and does not explain why results happened. Non-financial information covers things such as occupancy, guest satisfaction scores, repeat bookings, staff turnover, complaints and energy use. It often comes from operating systems and surveys, can be collected daily, and frequently gives early warning of what will later show up in the money figures. Its limits are that some measures, such as satisfaction, are harder to check and can be collected in inconsistent ways. A hotel needs both. A good profit in one month may hide falling guest satisfaction that will cut future bookings, while high occupancy at heavy discounts may look good but earn little profit. Using both, as a balanced scorecard does, lets the general manager see current results and the drivers of future results, and act before problems reach the bottom line.
markingPoints: Defines financial information with examples and its main limits
Defines non-financial information with relevant hotel examples and its limits
Explains that non-financial measures can give early warning of financial results
Uses an example showing how one type alone could mislead
Concludes with a clear reason why both are needed, for example a balanced scorecard

essays.stem: Explain how you would present a monthly performance report so that busy managers can understand it quickly and act on it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would open with a one-page summary that states the main results, the three or four issues that need decisions, and my recommendations. Below that, a dashboard would show the agreed key measures against target and last year, using red, amber and green to flag items outside the agreed limits, so managers can see at once where to look. I would use the right chart for each purpose: line graphs for trends over time, bar charts for comparing branches, and tables only where exact figures are needed. Axes would start at zero and scales would be the same from month to month so that charts do not mislead. Every page would use the same units, periods and layout. Beside each key movement I would write a short commentary explaining the cause and its effect, in plain language, with technical terms explained. Detailed schedules would go into an appendix for those who want them. Finally, I would send the report on the agreed date, in the format each manager prefers, and offer a short briefing to answer questions.
markingPoints: Starts with a short summary of results, issues and recommendations
Shows key measures against target with exceptions highlighted
Chooses suitable charts and avoids misleading displays
Keeps a consistent layout and adds plain-language commentary on causes
Puts detail in appendices and delivers on time in the agreed format

essays.stem: Describe how you would protect confidential and personal information when providing financial and business performance information to managers.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would find out which information is confidential: pay and personal details of staff, customer account data, prices and contracts, and results not yet released to the board or the public. I would follow the organisation's information policy and the general aims of the data protection law, which require personal data to be used only for a proper purpose, kept to what is needed, kept accurate and kept secure. In practice I would give each manager only the information they are authorised to see, for example pay totals by department rather than named salaries, unless they are authorised to see named figures. Reports would be stored in folders with access controls, and spreadsheets holding personal data would be password protected. I would send reports through the firm's secure systems, never from personal email, and check the recipient list before sending. Printed copies would be collected from the printer at once and shredded when no longer needed. If someone asked for information they were not entitled to, I would politely refuse and refer them to the authorised manager. Any breach would be reported straight away under the policy.
markingPoints: Identifies which kinds of information are confidential or personal
Refers to policy and the general aims of the data protection law
Limits each report to what the user is authorised and needs to see
Uses secure storage, access controls and secure sending
Handles unauthorised requests and breaches correctly

essays.stem: Evaluate the limits of using ratios and trends to judge a business's performance, and say how a manager should allow for them.
essays.modelAnswer: Ratios and trends are useful because they turn many figures into a few measures that can be compared over time and with other firms. However, they have important limits. They are only as reliable as the data behind them, so errors, late entries or changes in accounting methods can distort them. They are based on past results and may not show what will happen next. A single period can be affected by one-off events such as a storm, a large order or a strike. Comparisons with other firms can mislead if those firms are a different size, use different methods or work in a different market. A ratio shows that something has changed but not why: a falling gross margin could come from higher costs, lower prices or a change in the sales mix. A manager should therefore check the data first, look at several periods rather than one, compare like with like, read the ratios together with non-financial measures and the commentary, and investigate the causes before acting. Ratios should prompt questions rather than give final answers.
markingPoints: Recognises the value of ratios and trends for comparison
Explains limits from data quality and changes in method
Explains limits from one-off events, past focus and unfair comparisons
Notes that ratios show what changed, not why
Gives sensible ways to allow for the limits, such as several periods, like-for-like comparison and investigation

essays.stem: Managers at a distribution firm say the monthly performance pack is 40 pages long, arrives three weeks after month end and is hard to use. Recommend how the reporting should be improved, and justify your recommendations.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first survey the managers to find which items they use, which they ignore and what they lack, and then agree a shorter set of key measures with each of them. Cutting the pack to a summary page, a dashboard and a few pages of commentary, with detail in an appendix or on request, would make it quicker to read and easier to act on. To speed it up, I would map the month-end steps and remove delays, for example by agreeing cut-off times with the data owners, using standard templates and linking the dashboard directly to the accounting system. A flash report of a few key figures within three working days, marked as unchecked, would give managers early warning while the full pack follows within ten working days. I would use exception reporting so that attention goes to items outside agreed limits. These changes are justified because information is only useful if it arrives in time to change decisions and is clear enough to be acted on. I would review the new format with users after three months.
markingPoints: Consults users to find what is used, ignored and missing
Recommends a shorter pack focused on key measures and exceptions
Recommends practical ways to speed up preparation
Justifies the changes by timeliness and usefulness for decisions
Plans a review of the new format with users

essays.stem: The manager of a public agency in Kingston must decide whether to keep cleaning in-house or contract it out. Describe the financial and non-financial information you would provide to support the decision, and how you would present it.
essays.modelAnswer: On the financial side, I would give the full current cost of in-house cleaning: wages and statutory contributions, supervision, supplies, equipment and its upkeep, and a share of overheads that would actually be saved. I would set this against the quoted contract prices, including GCT at the current rate where it applies, and add the cost of managing the contract and any one-off costs such as staff redundancy or transfer. I would show the figures over three years, not just one, and state my assumptions. On the non-financial side, I would provide current quality measures such as inspection scores and complaints, the risks to service and security of having outside staff on site, the effect on current staff and their morale, and the need to follow the procurement rules for public bodies. I would present a one-page comparison table of the options with the net cost difference, a short list of risks with ratings, and a clear note of what is uncertain. I would not make the decision for the manager but would set out the evidence fairly so that she can make it.
markingPoints: Gives a full in-house cost, including costs that would be saved
Compares with contract prices and extra costs of contracting out, over more than one year
Includes relevant non-financial information: quality, risks, staff and procurement rules
States assumptions and uncertainty
Presents the options clearly and fairly for the manager to decide

essays.stem: Recommend five key performance indicators for the food and beverage department of a resort hotel in Ocho Rios, and justify each one.
essays.modelAnswer: First, food cost percentage, which is food cost as a share of food sales. It shows whether purchasing, portion control and waste are under control, and it can be checked weekly against a target. Second, revenue per cover (average spend per guest), which shows whether staff are selling well and whether menu prices are right. Third, guest satisfaction score from comment cards or online reviews, because repeat business and the hotel's reputation depend on it, and it gives early warning before revenue falls. Fourth, labour cost as a percentage of sales, since staff are the largest cost after food and rostering must match busy and quiet times. Fifth, waste in kilograms or J$ per week, which links cost control to the hotel's environmental goals and can be improved quickly by the team. Each KPI should have a clear definition, a target, a named owner and a source of data, and be reported on the department's dashboard against target and last year. Together they balance cost, sales, service and sustainability rather than looking only at profit.
markingPoints: Names five relevant and measurable KPIs for the department
Justifies each by what it shows and how managers can act on it
Includes a balance of financial and non-financial measures
States that each KPI needs a definition, target, owner and data source
Explains how the KPIs will be reported

practical1.title: Prepare a monthly business performance pack for a manager
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a data pack for a made-up organisation (for example a hardware store chain with three branches in Kingston, Mandeville and Montego Bay, or a parish health centre): twelve months of sales, costs and budget figures, staff numbers, complaints and other operating records, and a short note from the general manager saying what she wants to know. The data contains three deliberate errors. As a group, check and correct the data, work out the agreed measures (for example sales growth, gross margin, cost per unit and complaints per 1,000 sales), build a one-page dashboard showing each measure against target and last year, and write a two-page commentary with recommendations. Give each member a named role: data checker (finds and records the errors and how they were fixed), analyst (works the ratios and percentages, checked twice by another member), chart builder (makes the dashboard and charts), commentary writer (drafts the explanation of causes and the recommendations), and quality reviewer (checks the finished pack against the manager's note). In a group of four, the analyst also reviews the pack. Photograph or screenshot each stage and hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Data pack and manager's note from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software, and a printer
photos: The flipchart plan showing roles, measures and deadlines
The error log listing the three errors found and how each was corrected
The calculation sheet on screen, with the second member's check marked
The one-page dashboard showing measures against target and last year
The quality reviewer's checklist signed off against the manager's note
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Found and corrected the errors before analysing the data
Ratios and percentages are correct and were checked twice
Charts suit the data and do not mislead (axes, scales, labels)
Commentary explains causes in plain language and gives realistic recommendations
The pack answers what the manager asked for
Explained their part clearly when the assessor asked
safety: Use only the made-up data in the pack and keep the work confidential to the group and the assessor
Save work to the Centre's folder and do not share login details
Share the workload fairly and agree realistic times for each part
Take short screen breaks and keep cables out of walkways

practical2.title: Agree information needs and brief managers on performance
practical2.brief: Your group plays the information team of a made-up organisation (for example a bus company in Spanish Town or an agency of a ministry). In part one, two assessors or volunteers play managers. Interview each manager for ten minutes to find out what decisions they make and what performance information they need, then write an information specification for each: the measures, source, format, frequency, deadline and who may see it. In part two, the assessor gives a short set of results. Prepare a ten-minute briefing with no more than six slides for the managers, present it, answer their questions, and record any follow-up actions. Give each member a named role: lead interviewer (runs the interviews), note-taker (records the managers' needs), specification writer (drafts the two specifications), slide designer (builds the slides from the results), and presenter (leads the briefing, with every member answering at least one question). In a group of four, the note-taker also writes the follow-up action list. Photograph each stage and hand in the notes, specifications, slides and action list.
materials: Manager role cards and a results sheet from the assessor
Computer with presentation software and a projector or large screen
photos: The interview questions prepared before the interviews
An interview in progress, with the note-taker recording (work area only if anyone prefers no face)
The slides on screen, including the summary slide
The briefing in progress with the managers' questions being answered
The follow-up action list with owners and dates
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Asked open questions that drew out the decisions each manager makes
Specifications record measures, sources, format, frequency, deadlines and access
Slides are clear, accurate and match the results given
Answered questions accurately and politely, without guessing figures
Recorded follow-up actions with owners and dates
Kept to time in the interviews and the briefing
safety: Treat the role-play information as confidential and do not use real people's data
Speak respectfully and let each person finish during interviews and questions
Ask permission before photographing anyone; photograph notes and screens if a person prefers
Share speaking and writing fairly and take a short break between the two parts
